prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "AbbVie Inc." (ticker ABBV), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ABBV", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: AbbVie Inc.
markets: Immunology (psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, atopic dermatitis)
Medical aesthetics (botulinum toxin and dermal fillers)

mission.statement: AbbVie's mission is to discover and deliver innovative medicines and solutions that solve serious health issues today and address the medical challenges of tomorrow.
mission.source: AbbVie company boilerplate (abbvie.com and 'About AbbVie' in its press releases)
mission.plain: Invent and supply medicines that treat serious illnesses now and in the future.

about.plain: AbbVie invents and sells prescription medicines. Its biggest sellers calm down an overactive immune system that causes skin, gut and joint diseases. It also makes medicines for mental health, migraines, Parkinson's and blood cancers. And it owns Botox, the shot used to smooth wrinkles and treat headaches.
about.customers: Patients get its medicines through doctors, hospitals, pharmacies and insurers, and beauty clinics buy its Botox and fillers.
about.everyday: Botox, the famous anti-wrinkle injection, is an AbbVie product, and its Skyrizi and Rinvoq ads run constantly on US TV.

money.plain: Skyrizi, Rinvoq and Humira for psoriasis, Crohn's, colitis and arthritis
Vraylar, Botox for migraine, Ubrelvy, Qulipta, Vyalev

money.part: New Parkinson's and cancer drug launches
money.plain: Vyalev pump for Parkinson's, tavapadon, and antibody-drug conjugates like Emrelis and Temab-A

result.summary: AbbVie has a real but patent-dependent advantage: it built Skyrizi and Rinvoq into the leading next-generation immunology franchise (FY2025 sales $17.6B and $8.3B) fast enough to replace Humira, whose sales collapsed after US biosimilars in 2023, and it owns the Botox brand. Its moat comes from patents, clinical data across many diseases, payer contracts and a huge commercial machine, not from anything permanent, so it must keep re-buying and re-inventing its portfolio.

pricingPower.evidence: Immunology growth is volume-driven: management said on the Q2 2026 call that contracting concessions are 'low single digit' on rebates and price, while Humira sales shrank to $4,540M in FY2025 after US biosimilars arrived in 2023 and Imbruvica fell 29% in Q2 2026 partly from IRA Medicare price setting.

moats.evidence: Patents and regulatory exclusivity on Skyrizi and Rinvoq (into the 2030s) plus the Botox brand, which is a household word, underpin about $26B of FY2025 Skyrizi/Rinvoq sales and $6.4B of Botox sales.

Patients stable on a biologic are rarely switched without failure and payers lock in formulary positions annually, but biosimilars showed with Humira that switching happens fast once a cheaper equivalent exists.
Medicines do not become more valuable as more people use them.
With $61.2B of FY2025 revenue and about $9.8B of planned 2026 adjusted R&D, AbbVie can run large multi-indication trials and a big US sales force that small rivals cannot match.
Immunology is crowded (J&J, Lilly, Novartis, UCB, Pfizer, BMS, Takeda), so its markets are not natural monopolies.
Its model is the same branded-pharma model as its rivals.
It proved it can manage a loss of exclusivity: management led revenue back to its peak within two years of the 2023 US Humira biosimilar entry by migrating patients to Skyrizi and Rinvoq.
Exclusive patents on its key molecules and Botox manufacturing know-how; neither is permanent.

customers.evidence: Skyrizi captures new and switching US psoriasis patients at a rate management says is 4x any other biologic or oral, and leads in more than 30 countries; Skyrizi sales are guided to $21.7B in 2026 from $17.6B in 2025.

talent.evidence: BioSpace lists AbbVie as a Best Place to Work every year 2022-2026 and it has been named on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For and more than 40 Great Place to Work and Top Employer lists.

product.evidence: Skyrizi beat Stelara and Otezla in head-to-head trials and Rinvoq has approvals across many immune diseases; Botox is the category-defining toxin.

competitors.name: Johnson & Johnson
competitors.note: Tremfya and Stelara versus Skyrizi in psoriasis and IBD; co-markets Imbruvica; Caplyta versus Vraylar in psychiatry.

competitors.name: Eli Lilly
competitors.note: Taltz, Omvoh and Ebglyss in psoriasis, colitis and atopic dermatitis; Jaypirca versus Imbruvica; migraine (Emgality).

competitors.name: Novartis
competitors.note: Cosentyx versus Skyrizi in psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis; Kesimpta and neuroscience.

competitors.name: Pfizer
competitors.note: Xeljanz versus Rinvoq (JAK inhibitors); Velsipity in colitis; Nurtec versus Ubrelvy in migraine.

competitors.name: Bristol Myers Squibb
competitors.note: Sotyktu in psoriasis, Zeposia in colitis, Cobenfy versus Vraylar in schizophrenia, blood cancers.

competitors.name: Amgen
competitors.note: Otezla in psoriasis, Amjevita Humira biosimilar, Aimovig in migraine.

competitors.name: UCB
competitors.note: Bimzelx IL-17 drug competes with Skyrizi in psoriasis and hidradenitis; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Sanofi / Regeneron
competitors.note: Dupixent versus Rinvoq in atopic dermatitis; Regeneron (REGN) co-owns it.

competitors.name: Takeda
competitors.note: Entyvio versus Skyrizi and Rinvoq in Crohn's disease and colitis.

competitors.name: AstraZeneca
competitors.note: Calquence versus Imbruvica in CLL; antibody-drug conjugates in solid tumors.

competitors.name: BeOne Medicines (BeiGene)
competitors.note: Brukinsa has taken BTK-inhibitor share from Imbruvica; sonrotoclax versus Venclexta.

competitors.name: Galderma
competitors.note: Dysport, Relfydess and Restylane versus Botox Cosmetic and Juvederm; does not file with the SEC.

competitors.name: Evolus
competitors.note: Jeuveau aesthetic toxin and Evolysse fillers targeting younger Botox customers.

competitors.name: Biosimilar makers (Sandoz, Amgen, Samsung Bioepis and others)
competitors.note: Humira biosimilars, and later Skyrizi/Rinvoq generics, erode AbbVie's older franchises.

estimates.name: Biosimilar makers (Sandoz, Amgen, Samsung Bioepis and others)

threats: US biosimilars for Skyrizi and Rinvoq once patents expire in the 2030s, repeating the Humira collapse
IRA Medicare price negotiation (already hitting Imbruvica) spreading to Vraylar, Botox and immunology drugs
New oral IL-23 pills (J&J's icotrokinra) and other orals competing with injectable Skyrizi
Heavy debt ($70.8B at June 2026) and acquisition dependence, e.g. the ~$10.9B Apogee deal, with risk of overpaying
Pipeline failures such as emraclidine in schizophrenia (2024) and weak aesthetics demand (Juvederm declining)
Pharmacy-benefit-manager and payer rebate pressure in immunology

ceo.name: Robert A. Michael
ceo.background: Accountant by training (BS accounting, Indiana University Kelley School of Business; MBA, UCLA Anderson); former AbbVie CFO, president and COO, began career at Abbott

c1.evidence: AbbVie leads next-generation immunology, a large and still growing field (Skyrizi $17.6B and Rinvoq $8.3B in FY2025), but pharma is not an emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Doctors pick Skyrizi and Rinvoq for strong head-to-head trial data and broad labels, an edge that lasts until patents expire in the 2030s, so it is durable but not permanent.

c3.evidence: Most people know Botox and Humira but not the AbbVie name; within immunology it is the default leader, with Skyrizi winning new psoriasis patients at 4x the rate of any rival per management.

c4.evidence: Its mission to 'discover and deliver innovative medicines' is standard pharma language and the company is known more for Humira's patent thicket and pricing than for purpose-driven leadership.

c6.evidence: “Humira, Botox, big pharma, drug prices” - AbbVie is respected for effective medicines but criticised for Humira's patent wall and high US prices, so the impression is mixed.

c7.evidence: Immunology, neuroscience and oncology are large markets growing with aging populations, and 2026 revenue guidance of about $67.6B is up ~10%, but there is no single secular tailwind like AI.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into Parkinson's (Vyalev, tavapadon), antibody-drug conjugates, new immunology indications (vitiligo, alopecia) and early obesity work, largely through acquisitions.

m1.evidence: Rob Michael has a clear plan built on Skyrizi/Rinvoq and pipeline deals, but it is a financial-portfolio vision rather than a transformative picture of the future.

m2.evidence: Michael is a professional manager promoted from CFO in 2024, not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no specific public evidence of a servant-leadership style beyond standard corporate messaging.

m5.evidence: AbbVie's culture is known for commercial execution and deal-making (Allergan, ImmunoGen, Cerevel, Apogee) more than for in-house invention.

m6.evidence: Michael is an accountant with an MBA whose career was in finance and commercial operations, not science.

m7.evidence: No controversy specific to Michael is known, but the company's Humira patent and pricing strategy drew congressional criticism.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Rob Michael at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: He keeps a low public profile typical of pharma CEOs.

m9.evidence: Under him as COO and CEO, revenue returned to growth within two years of Humira's 2023 US loss of exclusivity, reaching $61,160M in FY2025 versus $54,318M in FY2023.

m10.evidence: AbbVie is not known for frugality; it spends heavily on marketing and large acquisitions.

c10.evidence: Its drugs help millions with psoriasis, Crohn's, arthritis, migraine and blood cancer, but mainly in rich countries and at high prices.

p2.evidence: Discovering, testing and manufacturing biologics and getting them through FDA trials across many diseases is extremely hard and important.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in 4 of the last 5 years ($45,804M in 2020 to $61,160M in 2025) but fell 6% in 2023 as Humira biosimilars launched.

f2.evidence: GAAP gross margin rose from 66.4% in 2020 to 70.2% in 2025, but operating margin fell from 31.9% in 2021 to 24.6% in 2025 due to acquired R&D and amortization charges.

f3.evidence: Debt was $70,822M against $6,569M of cash at June 30, 2026, and stockholders' equity was negative ($-5,935M).

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $11,363M in 2020 to $15,075M in 2025 but dipped to $12,757M in 2023 and $9,137M in 2024; operating cash flow was not checked here.

v1.evidence: Skyrizi beat Stelara and Otezla head-to-head and is the top-prescribed IL-23 drug, but rivals like Tremfya, Cosentyx and Bimzelx are close alternatives.

v2.evidence: AbbVie appears on BioSpace Best Places to Work every year 2022-2026 and on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For list.

c5.evidence: Millions of patients with psoriasis, Crohn's disease, arthritis, migraine and leukemia rely on its drugs and would need to switch therapies if it vanished, though rivals could fill most gaps.
